Applicant's agreement with the SCWMRD regarding Bad Creek mitigation measures indicates that another pumped storage plant may be needed by 1995. Future use of these reservoirs for power purposes would further impact existing temperature regimes, probably further reducing the coldwater habitat in Lake Jocassee.
Operation of the project could attract trouc and other fish to the area of the inlet-outlet structure through the influence of water currents and increased food brought about by fish killed by generating. This clustering of fish could lead to increased entrainment during pumping. A monitoring program should be developed to determine the effect of project operation on entrainment and subsequent mortality of fish. Such studies should include evaluation of the extent of the Bad Creek discharge plume and its impact on nursery areas, fish migration, and fish spawning.
9.3 WILDLIFE
The proposed project would result in the loss of about 505 acres of wildlife habitat, including 370 acres within the impoundment area. Wildlife inhabiting this area would be forced to migrate to adjacent areas, or perish. If the new areas of habitat are at their carrying capacity, displaced wildlife would be lost.
Definite measures to mitigate or compensate for losses of wildlife habitat have not been proposed. Interior has commended the Applicant for its cooperation in leasing Keowee-Toxaway Project lands to the SCWMRD for wildlife management purposes, but Interior questions whether or not such measures would fully compensate for the expected loss of wildlife associated with the proposed Bad Creek Project. The PPC Staff concludes that a mitigation plan should be developed to offset expected losses of wildlife resources. It is possible that the "Missouri System" (Daniel and Lamaire, 1974) could be followed in planning mitigation for these losses.
The Applicant, in coordination with SCWMRD could effect such wildlife mitigation by a program of intensive management on land adjacent to the project. The management objectives would include increasing the wildlife carrying capacity. Staff believes that population studies should be conducted before and after project implementation, at least for the principal game species (i.e., deer, turkey, and bear).
